/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.headline: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil
/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.excerpt: After the first round of the Brazilian presidential election three weeks ago, the leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva reportedly told allies he could not understand how he finished second after a government he considered the best of his three terms. A mood of dismay swept Brazil’s left, and because 9 million voters for the other candidates, all of them on the right, were expected to mostly transfer to senator Flávio Bolsonaro, analysts widely saw the far-right senator’s victory as certain. Then, on the night after the election, students from the Fluminense Federal University took to the streets of Niterói, a city of 480,000 across Guanabara Bay from Rio de Janeiro, to protest against the return to power of a member of the Bolsonaro family, whose patriarch, former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father, is under house arrest for attempting a coup. Two days later, another student protest took over downtown Rio and, in the days that followed, similar ones spread across the country in organic demonstrations that analysts and Lula himself agree gave new life to his campaign and played a decisive role in his historic comeback in the runoff. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech on Sunday night after defeating Bolsonaro.
/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.trail: A viral WhatsApp channel and student-led protests played a key role in the veteran Brazilian leftist’s election victory

/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.headline: Brazil keeps left: what Lula’s victory means for his country and beyond
/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.excerpt: Good morning. Chances are you woke this morning to news of two momentous election results. In Serbia, a student-led movement has ousted the country’s long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić (which you can read more about here). And just hours ago, Brazil’s president staged a sensational turnaround against his far-right opponent after a nail-biting vote. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, won a forth nonconsecutive term as president, seeing off far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who spearheaded the radical populist movement built by his father and former president, Jair. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election. After Bolsonaro’s surprise first-round victory earlier this month, the Workers’ party incumbent Lula pulled off a historic fightback – a consolidation of the democratic resurgence the country has enjoyed since he took office – and an early birthday present for the veteran leftist, who turns 81 on Tuesday. But with Bolsonaro refusing to accept the result, the victory is a tense one. I spoke to the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips, who was in São Paulo at the Workers’ party vote count, to find out what the result means and what may lie ahead. Weekend roundup UK news | Two people have been killed and more than 160,000 properties have been left without power as Storm Boelo continues to batter the UK.
/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.trail: In today’s newsletter: As Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured victory in the presidential race, we look the implications for democracy, the environment and international relations

/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.headline: More than one million Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff
/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.excerpt: More than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro. Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%. On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back. Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president, who was first elected in 2002, would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.” “The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students. “Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.
/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.trail: Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro

/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.headline: ‘Bolso shows all signs of fascism’: the journalist who predicted Brazil’s future – and paid the ultimate price
/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.excerpt: “Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters,” the murdered British journalist Dom Phillips told me before his death. “His sons are all more extreme if anything.” These words were written in 2018 by the Guardian contributor shortly before the election of the far-right former army captain Jair Bolsonaro as president of Brazil – a prospect that Dom viewed with dread. As he predicted back then, this would lead to more mortalities, more destruction of the Amazon rainforest and more danger for journalists. His own life and death were to prove the prescience of this foresight. Dom was killed four years ago alongside the Brazilian indigenous expert Bruno Pereira, but his views feel alarmingly relevant once more as Brazil braces for a presidential runoff this Sunday in which a member of the far-right Bolsonaro clan is once more a favourite to win – despite all the dangers that poses to the environment and those who seek to protect it. Polls suggest Flávio Bolsonaro – the son of Jair Bolsonaro – is narrowly ahead of the Workers party incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Although the difference between them is within the margin of error and Lula appears to have gained momentum, the possibility of another Bolsonaro administration is likely to fill any friends of Dom and Bruno with alarm. Dom was no diehard political leftist.
/world/2026/oct/26/brazil-lula-vow-democ.trail: Dom Phillips warned that Jair Bolsonaro would make life more dangerous for reporters and the Amazon rainforest, and that his sons were even more extreme

/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.headline: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.excerpt: On Tuesday Israel holds its first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks, the deadliest day in the country’s history, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians. Since then Israel has pursued a war of annihilation in Gaza, launched two inconclusive wars with Iran, and intensified a campaign of state-backed ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank. Domestically the coalition formed by Benjamin Netanyahu has taken aim at democratic institutions, including the supreme court. Many Israelis have described this election as the most consequential in their country’s history. Who are the main players? The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has led Israel for 19 out of the last 30 years, most recently at the head of a far-right coalition. He is seeking a new mandate with the endorsement of the US president, Donald Trump, and the fight is personal as well as political. He is on trial for corruption; losing power may mean a greater risk of jail time. His main rival is Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israeli military and relative political newcomer, the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to the heart of Israel’s establishment from humble beginnings. His son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza in 2024. He lacks Netanyahu’s charisma, but has embraced that as part of a campaign positioning him as the opposite of Israel’s current leader, down to the name of his new party – Yashar, or “Honesty”.
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.trail: Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking a new mandate in Israel’s first election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks

/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.headline: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.excerpt: Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote. A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left. They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation. Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises. As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.trail: Families forced to flee as Netanyahu tries to prove security credentials after two Israeli soldiers killed days before election

/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.headline: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.excerpt: Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said. The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry. Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags. People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters. The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20-minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed. Israeli elections will take place in four days and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.trail: PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint

/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.headline: ‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder’: Palestinians fear the worst from Israel election
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.excerpt: As Israel prepares to go to the polls, Palestinians in Gaza are bracing for an outcome that could shape their future, knowing their fate rests with the country that has reduced much of the territory to rubble and killed nearly 75,000 people. Gaza, where nearly a million displaced Palestinians face dire sanitary conditions, water shortages and the constant threat of Israeli strikes, has been largely absent from the election campaign. Both Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition Yashar party have focused instead on the goal of destroying Hamas in the wake of the 7 October attacks and the trauma inflicted on Israeli society. The humanitarian catastrophe unfolding just across the border has received little, if any, attention. “We hope a government will come to power that is less inclined towards killing, displacement and our extermination,” said Sami Abu Rumi, 47, from Rafah, who is now displaced in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. “But, ultimately, we see the thinking of Israeli governments as largely similar.” Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has set out a clear plan for Gaza’s future. Both have vowed to end Hamas rule and both support Donald Trump’s controversial peace plan. Eisenkot, the former military chief whose party is leading Netanyahu’s Likud in the polls, has pledged to restore Israel’s international standing after three years of war. Yet he is no dove.
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.trail: Humanitarian catastrophe largely ignored as rivals Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu vow to end Hamas rule

/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.headline: Israel launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killed
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.excerpt: Israel has launched a campaign of collective punishment against Palestinians in Hebron after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three near a checkpoint outside the city. Benjamin Netanyahu announced a siege on Hebron and neighbouring Halhul and said residents of the gunmen’s home neighbourhoods would all be forced out. He promised mass demolitions of homes. The first destruction began within hours of the attack, as ministers who had been on the campaign trail ahead of elections on Tuesday rushed to the site of the shooting. The far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, posted a video of himself in front of a bulldozer as it tore down a Palestinian home near the site of the firefight. The destruction of a home built without permits aimed to “create deterrence and exact a price”, Smotrich said. There was no claim of a connection between the building’s owners and the attackers. Soon after the destruction began, Israel’s high court issued a temporary order to stop the demolitions. A human rights lawyer, Mohammed Dahleh, filed an urgent petition on behalf of two factory owners nearby, arguing that the demolition violated international law on collective punishment and Israeli administrative law. “What we saw today was an attempt to copy the illegal practices used in Gaza, in the heart of the West Bank,” Dahleh said.
/world/2026/oct/26/netanyahu-reportedly-.trail: Benjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfight

/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.headline: Retail sales in Great Britain fall as struggling households cut back
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.excerpt: Retail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor, John Healey, announces his budget next week. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall. The decrease, which was fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter wear because of an unseasonably warm September, comes as figures show consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate since the Covid pandemic. While retail sales dropped across almost all sectors of the industry, the volume of motor fuel sold soared 2.2% month on month despite prices at the pump hitting record highs, returning to levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East. In value terms, the 6.1% increase in fuel sales was the biggest month-on-month increase since 10.9% was recorded in March, the month immediately after the start of the US-Iran conflict. Stripping out the increase from fuel, retail sales fell 0.7% in September, much worse than the 0.1% fall forecast by the City. “October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner,” said Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics.
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.trail: Latest negative economic update comes as John Healey prepares to announce budget next week

/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.headline: UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Brexit vote as cost of living bites
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.excerpt: Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain. With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living. Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum. The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown. The latest snapshot represents a marked change from the summer, when GfK said a “Burnham bounce”, along with a strong World Cup run by the men’s England football team and sunny weather, lifted the mood of consumers in its long-running monthly survey.
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.trail: Economic fallout from war in Middle East adds to pressures on consumers and on chancellor before budget

/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.headline: Sainsbury’s expects challenging run-up to Christmas as households feel squeeze
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.excerpt: Sainsbury’s has warned of a “pretty challenging” market in the run-up to Christmas as households are “finding it tough” and food producers face rising costs. Simon Roberts, the chief executive of the UK’s second biggest supermarket, called on the government not to “further aggravate” pressure on costs for business in this month’s budget. He said it was “important this government does not repeat what we have seen in previous budgets” in raising business rates and employers’ national insurance contributions. “That’s been really hard,” he said. After Sainsbury’s and other industry leaders met government ministers last week, Roberts said he believed “this government is really listening to business” especially on helping to create more jobs for young people. Roberts added that food inflation was not “anything like” some of the high levels forecast earlier in the year but suggested high energy and fertiliser costs could push up food prices next year. Roberts said that in a more unsettled global environment the UK needed to “improve food resilience and grow and produce more at home”. He called on the government to increase tax breaks that support investment in technology – including irrigation and reservoirs – on farms, as the climate crisis is expected to lead to more hotter, drier summers such as this year’s.
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.trail: Supermarket urges government not to ‘further aggravate’ pressure on costs for businesses in next week’s budget

/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.headline: Jumping beans: UK shoppers turn to legumes to save cash and improve diet
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.excerpt: British shoppers are munching more beans, lentils, tofu and tempeh – while cutting back on real and plant-based fake meat – to save money and improve their diet. The amount of beans, pulses and soya bean derivatives sold in the UK increased by 7.3% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, led by a rise in cheap dried lentils, an analysis has found. That was led by a 23% surge for cheap dried lentils, according to data from the market research firm NielsenIQ evaluated by the climate advocacy group Madre Brava. Shoppers turned to more upmarket legumes, including organic and jarred varieties, with sales of canned and jarred butter beans up by 30.3%. That growth was partly driven by new products and brands – such as the Bold Bean Co, Navarrico and Marks & Spencer’s own-label – as well as recipes going viral on social media. Baked beans, once the titans of the supermarket tinned section, initially appeared to have become has-beens in the frenzy, with 1.2% fewer cans sold – but the decline is actually down to a drop in cans also containing sausages. Fake meats, once seen as the future of vegetarian and vegan diets, also continue to fall out of favour, with 4.3% fewer packages sold. The decline was down to sales of textured soya, pea and wheat protein products, which offset a renewed growth in mycoprotein – sold under the brand name Quorn.
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.trail: Sales of beans, lentils and soya bean derivatives on rise while Britons buy less real and fake meat

/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.headline: Consumer confidence at near two-year high as World Cup and UK holidaying lift summer spending
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.excerpt: Consumer confidence hit its highest level in almost two years in July, according to research that indicated the closing stages of the men’s football World Cup and more people holidaying in the UK raised summer spending. A truce in the Middle East conflict in June and the arrival of a new prime minister in No 10 also gave a lift to consumers after a long period of heightened uncertainty. A long-running monthly consumer spending survey by Barclays showed that 30% of those surveyed felt confident about the strength of the UK economy in July – representing a 21-month high and a six-percentage-point improvement on June. Consumer card spending grew by 2% year on year last month, after a 1.9% increase in June, Barclays said. The bank said the study showed people felt more secure in their jobs and had more leeway to spend on non-essentials, with discretionary spending up 1.6%. Among the biggest beneficiaries were pubs, which enjoyed a 10% increase in transactions “thanks to England’s World Cup run”. It had been estimated that the tournament had brought in £150m in added sales for British pubs. Card spending at cinemas rose 2.6%, helped by the popularity of Toy Story 5 and The Odyssey – the highest grossing movie of the film-maker Christopher Nolan’s career. In line with other surveys of economic activity, the report found that the succession of heatwaves had depressed spending on airline tickets in favour of domestic holidays, which pushed up spending on UK accommodation by 2.6%.
/business/2026/oct/27/uk-shop-price-infl.trail: Barclays says survey shows people feel more secure in jobs and have more leeway to spend on non-essentials

/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.headline: EU leaders to press Burnham to pay more towards Ukraine’s defence
/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.excerpt: EU leaders will press Andy Burnham at a summit in Brussels to contribute more to Ukraine’s defence effort in 2027. EU officials argue that the UK, Canada and Japan should do more to support Ukraine, but entreaties to these G7 countries for extra financial aid at recent international meetings have not been answered, Brussels says. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, will call on the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, to contribute to Ukraine’s looming financial shortfall at an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next week. A similar request to the British prime minister will be made when he meets von der Leyen and the European Council president, António Costa, for a long-awaited EU-UK summit on 20 November in Brussels. It comes as the UK chancellor, John Healey, prepares for his first budget next week, weighing numerous calls for more spending against the rising cost of government borrowing and a darkening economic outlook. Healey said earlier this month he was “working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine – military, diplomatic and economic”. Ukraine says it faces a €70bn (£58bn) funding shortfall in 2027 to pay for its defence and civilian needs. The EU and its member states are paying for 80% of Ukraine’s financial needs, according to the commission, which considers a “fair” EU share to be two-thirds, with the remaining third covered by other allies.
/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.trail: Officials will call on UK to ‘step up’ financial support at Brussels summit – with post-Brexit issues also on agenda

/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.headline: Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?
/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.excerpt: In February 2016, days after David Cameron announced the UK would hold a referendum on leaving the EU, he told workers in Slough not to imagine they could change their minds a few years down the line if they did not like how things panned out. Voting to stay in or leave was a once in a generation thing, he said. “This is a decision that lasts for life.” Well times change, as the last prime minister but five could testify. A decade after Britain told Brussels where to go, Brexit is back on the political agenda. After years in which many politicians avoided any mention of the B-word, Andy Burnham broke the omertà in his party conference speech last month, saying he would look again at Britain’s relationship with Europe. This week he went further, insisting the current arrangement must change: “Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain.” Among a range of options on the table, he has been clear, is the possibility of going “all the way” and rejoining the EU. There are pressing economic reasons Burnham has been talking up closer alignment, as the EU works out its position on the UK’s access to its protectionist “Made in Europe” legislation, which the prime minister has said could hurt British manufacturing. But after years of bitter division and political dysfunction in the fallout from the vote, are the British public really ready to talk about Brexit again – and even to contemplate reversing it? Polling evidence may suggest so.
/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.trail: As Andy Burnham talks up closer alignment with the EU and a poll suggests half in UK would rejoin, the B-word is back on the agenda

/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.headline: Repairing Brexit economic damage should be Burnham’s top priority, business chief says
/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.excerpt: Repairing the economic damage of Brexit should be the top priority for Andy Burnham as he reconsiders Labour’s red lines on EU membership, the head of one of Britain’s leading business groups has said. Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said she welcomed the prime minister reopening the Brexit battle lines despite the uncertainty it could create, arguing that the UK’s current trading relationship with the EU was bad for business. “We do think it’s right, because of what we know from the evidence of how businesses feel it’s not working,” she said. Highlighting the continuing economic hit from Brexit, Haviland said more than half of bosses surveyed by the business lobby group believed the deal negotiated by Boris Johnson’s government and enacted in 2021 was not helping them. “We expected it to be very difficult at the beginning, when [companies] were getting used to the new rules, and then it would sort of get easier as it went to along. But actually, that has not happened,” she said. Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far, with national income per head between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been had the UK not left the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a long-term hit of about 4% of gross domestic product. At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” as he pledged to reassess Britain’s relationship with the EU.
/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.trail: Shevaun Haviland argues PM is right to revisit Labour’s EU red lines as current trading relationship is bad for business

/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.headline: Burnham v Swinney: will the UK PM overshadow the SNP’s conference?
/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.excerpt: This year, even Andy Burnham is invited to the Scottish National party conference. But by the time John Swinney stands up to address members on Saturday afternoon in Aberdeen to reinvigorate the case for a second independence referendum, his party may regret giving the UK prime minister so much prominence in the conference buildup. Burnham is expected to visit Scotland on Friday – the middle of the event – in a thinly veiled attempt to overshadow the SNP gathering. While he will be in a different venue, the former Manchester mayor’s presence in Scotland will loom large over the event. Since taking over at No 10 in July, Burnham has largely avoided direct confrontations with his political rivals, rarely attacking Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch. But he has taken a different approach with the Scottish first minister. The SNP leader was the only politician from a rival party, apart from Margaret Thatcher, that Burnham mentioned in his keynote address to the Labour party conference last month. He reflected on Swinney’s prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK at a meeting of separatist parties Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to mark the first time all three devolved parliaments were governed by nationalists. Swinney inadvertently did so on the day Burnham’s father died. “I quote that not to seek sympathy,” Burnham said, holding back tears. “Nor to criticise John Swinney. I relay it because I want you to know how it made me feel.
/politics/2026/oct/26/andy-burnham-brexi.trail: Prime minister presents new kind of challenge for SNP, and his Scottish visit will loom large over its big event

/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.headline: Minister insists she backs migration policy after joking she couldn’t lie about supporting it
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.excerpt: The energy secretary has been forced to clarify that she backs Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy, after earlier joking that she had not been able to “lie” about supporting a key element of the changes. Miatta Fahnbulleh made the original remarks to a journalists’ event in Westminster, referring to an “awkward” Sky News interview in which she repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency. She told the event: “I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments, including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge yesterday.” The implication that she could not bring herself to lie about supporting the changes appears to have gone down badly among colleagues in government, although No 10 refused to be drawn on whether they requested her to issue a clarification. Fahnbulleh posted a statement on social media on Thursday evening saying: “Today I made what was meant to be a lighthearted, self-deprecating remark. I didn’t get it right and it hasn’t come off as I intended. “I fully support our home secretary and the government’s position on migration reform.
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.trail: Miatta Fahnbulleh says reference to ‘awkward’ interview was meant to be lighthearted and self-deprecating

/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.headline: Shabana Mahmood urged to ‘read the room’ on Labour opposition to immigration policy
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.excerpt: Shabana Mahmood has been urged to “read the room” on Labour opposition to her immigration policy, as No 10 declined to rule out watering down her plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency. Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards. She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule. However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.” There is already a cabinet split over the policy, which deepened on Wednesday when Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, repeatedly refused to back the specific plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency in the UK. This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed.
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.trail: No 10 declines to rule out watering down plans to extend waiting period for indefinite leave to remain as cabinet split widens

/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.headline: Home Office lifts deportation order for man, 62, who has lived in UK for 50 years
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.excerpt: The Home Office has lifted a deportation order handed to a 62-year-old man who has lived in Britain for 50 years after criticism of the department’s attempts to remove him to Barbados, a country he left as a child. The Home Office wrote to Tony Hall on Tuesday to inform him that his deportation order had been revoked. His case had been highlighted in the Guardian a day earlier. Hall had repeatedly tried to get the deportation order lifted, arguing that as the child of parents who emigrated to the Britain as part of the Windrush generation, he had the right to remain in the UK. He has no surviving relatives in Barbados and has not visited the country since arriving in London aged 12 to join his parents and five older sisters in 1976. The Home Office had previously stated that he was liable for deportation because of a 2001 conviction for conspiracy to rob and having a firearm with intent. Police stopped Hall and his co-defendants before the robbery was committed. Hall spent eight years in prison. Officials have been attempting to deport him since the end of his sentence in 2009. As a result of his precarious immigration status, he has been prohibited from working, renting somewhere to live, receiving benefits or receiving full access to NHS treatment. Hall had argued that he should not continue to be punished as a result of a crime committed 25 years ago, and for which he had served prison time.
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.trail: Department drops efforts to return Tony Hall to Barbados, a country he left at 12 and where he has no living relatives

/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.headline: Home Office denies British baby living in Thailand chance to meet great-grandfather in UK
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.excerpt: The Home Office has denied a great-grandfather from Lancashire the chance of meeting his five-month-old British great-grandson, who lives abroad. William Cross was born in Thailand on 30 April to parents Matthew Cross, 31, who is from Burnley in Lancashire, and Khin Thant Zin, known as Jue Jue, also 31, a refugee who fled persecution in Myanmar to Thailand. The family live on the island of Koh Tao, famous for its diving schools and a centre for turtle conservation. It is a popular tourism spot and Cross, a mechanical engineer, opened a steakhouse restaurant there 15 months ago. He met Zin on the island and the couple are now engaged. She works in the restaurant managing social media and human resources. Cross’s parents have visited the family in Thailand and have met their grandson. But William’s great-grandfather George Kerr, 74, who lives in Clayton-le-Moors in Lancashire, has multiple health problems and so is unable to fly out to Thailand to meet the baby. Instead, a large family gathering was planned in Burnley for Christmas. Cross said: “My grandfather suffers from ill health and sadly he is unable to travel. He and I have been extremely close all my life and I’m desperate for him to meet his [great] grandchild.” The family have just signed a lease on a new home and have bought some land on the island for later development. They assumed that organising a short trip to the UK for a family Christmas would be straightforward.
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.trail: British father would like to take his family to Lancashire to see ill relative but officials refused visa for his partner, a refugee from Myanmar

/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.headline: UK law could deny Fayed accusers recognition as victims of human trafficking
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.excerpt: Survivors of sexual violence could wrongly be denied recognition as victims of human trafficking under credibility tests in a new UK law, the independent anti-slavery commissioner has warned. Eleanor Lyons said the measures in the immigration and asylum bill were fundamentally unfair and could lead to many more victims of slavery and trafficking, including those allegedly abused by Mohamed Al Fayed, being denied support. Under the legislation, Home Office officials must regard any delay to making a claim of modern day slavery or human trafficking as damaging to their credibility. Any inaccuracy, inconsistency or omission in a person’s account, as well as any striking similarity to a claim made by someone else, must also be viewed as reasons for disbelief. Lyons said the credibility tests would harm survivors of sexual violence who often suffered memory loss as a result of their trauma. Many were also reluctant to come forward to disclose their exploitation due to fear of reprisals by their abusers, she added. “They are basically saying to victims, if you don’t come forward in a timely fashion not yet defined, if there are inconsistencies in your account, and if there are similarities between exploitation and [those of] others, the Home Office decision-maker must question your credibility,” Lyons said.
/politics/2026/oct/27/digital-hostile-en.trail: ‘Unfair’ immigration and asylum bill could fail to support sexual violence survivors, anti-slavery commissioner says
